title: Houthi Missiles Strike Yemen’s Presidential Palace in Aden; Toll Disputed
excerpt: The first strike on the seat of Yemen’s government in this conflict hit the Al-Maashiq palace while the prime minister and cabinet were inside; they were unharmed, and casualty figures range from two to four killed.
body:
• Houthi missiles struck the Al-Maashiq presidential palace in Aden on Thursday — the first strike on Yemen's seat of government in the current conflict, Reuters reported.
  • The death toll is disputed: AFP-sourced reporting put it at 4 killed and 10 wounded, while Reuters and CNN reported 2 guards from the prime minister's security detail killed.
  • Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani and his cabinet, who were inside, were unharmed; Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said five missiles were fired at the palace.
  • The Houthis said they targeted a Saudi military operations headquarters and weapons depots inside the palace complex.

Houthi missiles hit Yemen's presidential palace in Aden on Thursday, in the first strike on the seat of the internationally recognised government in the current conflict. Explosions were heard across the southern port city and smoke rose from the Al-Maashiq palace complex, witnesses told Reuters.

Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani and his cabinet were inside the palace and were unharmed, officials said. Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said five missiles were fired at the complex; Yemen's cabinet said the attack involved both missiles and drones.

A Disputed Toll

How many died is not yet settled. Government military sources told AFP — in reporting carried by NDTV — that four people were killed and ten wounded. Reuters and CNN put the toll at two killed, members of the prime minister's security detail; ANI, citing Al Arabiya, reported two security guards killed and six wounded. The Videshi is reporting the range until Yemeni officials publish a confirmed figure.

What the Houthis Say They Hit

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group's forces targeted a Saudi military operations headquarters — described as led by Saudi officers — and weapons depots inside the palace, under a declared policy of striking Saudi military build-ups wherever they are located. Yemen's cabinet said the attack would not affect government operations or its campaign against the Houthis, and Youth Minister Nayef Saleh al-Bakri said ministers would not leave Aden.

The Saudi-led coalition said Thursday's attacks showed the continuing Houthi threat to Saudi Arabia, regional security and shipping, and that operations to degrade Houthi capabilities would continue. The coalition also said it intercepted a drone over Khamis Mushait, a cruise missile over the Medina region and a drone in the Eastern Province on Thursday. Government forces said the Houthis also fired several ballistic missiles at Marib, the strategic oil-rich city in central Yemen, the same day.

Why This Strike Is Different

Houthi fire on Saudi airports and oil facilities has become a grim rhythm of this war's latest phase — it is why India's embassy in Riyadh updated its safety advisory for Indians in the kingdom on Thursday. A barrage aimed at the palace housing Yemen's own prime minister and cabinet is an escalation of a different kind: the government the Houthis are fighting, hit at its seat, in the interim capital. That the prime minister walked away unharmed may matter less than the message the missiles were sent to deliver.
